She speaks of the departure and transfers of some Sisters. She is alone and very busy. She asks her to look into a basket that was sent.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I hear what you tell me about the Sister and I have received the letter too; how dreadful! I always told you so, and I was not wrong; well, send her to me at once, for charity's sake, have her leave with Sr. A. Battistina.1

  2. Listen, I am sending three religious to Genoa; among them there is an old one, not old, but a widow, whom I think would suit you well; you will see her; if there is one there, send me one.2

  3. The one you say should be sent to the house at S. P. d'Arena, I would say no, because it would be a mess if she were to tell the mistress something, being so cunning; whereas in Genoa she can do nothing; so send her to Genoa, where they are in extreme need;3 and as soon as you receive this letter of mine, send me the two sisters.

Goodbye in haste; I have so much work that you cannot imagine it; I do not know where to lay my head, it aches so; I really think it is the work.

  1. I am alone at the desk, so to speak, and it is 11 o'clock and I have already written 5 letters, all very long. What can I do? Sr. A. Carlotta I send to Poss's every day, where there were immense muddles, and so Sr. A. Benedetta goes round now to one [side], now to the other;4 in short, I am always alone at this sorrowful desk where all the good and the bad come down, but the good is a speck and the bad and the sorrow are a great deal, so that I see they are now consuming me.5 Fiat.

  2. May God give you strength and courage and pour His blessings abundantly upon you.

6. Listen, do me the kindness of tracing the mistress's basket, for I hear she has not yet received it and needs it badly; and also the things belonging to those two I sent you: inside there was a bundle meant for Anna Grasso.6 For charity's sake, see about sending it to us at once, because it matters a great deal to me.

Goodbye, your affect. [Mother]

I hope you have received my letter.

She encloses the dispatch note for a parcel sent to her and tells her that two Sisters are coming.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I enclose a dispatch note for you to give to Fr Antonio Accinelli; it is for the dispatch of 4 capons, two for him and two for you;1 and I let you know that on Thursday you will receive two Sisters.

  2. You will go and fetch them at the station; they leave here at 9, and I think they arrive in Genoa a few minutes after 4.

  3. Thank you for everything you sent me; in these Sisters' luggage you will find linen for the house, for the kitchen and the table.2

Goodbye, I am in a hurry your affect. M. The Lord bless you all. Pray.

Three religious will be arriving. She asks her to find out about the things she has sent.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Just a line; listen, you will receive three religious: two are for you and one for S. P. D'Arena, the red-haired one, who is from Ovada, Sr. A. Laura.1

  2. I hope the things belonging to the others I sent have arrived;2 and the basket of the mistress at S. P. D'Arena, mention it to the Superior, and the bundle that was meant for the Grasso girl.3 I am sure they will not have been lost.

Goodbye, I am tired your affect. M. Rosa. God bless you all.

She introduces the two sisters she has assigned to the Lugo community, asking her to fit them into the school work. She speaks of the others who will be arriving for the new community at Mercatello and tells her what to ask the Archpriest about the teaching certificates needed for his school.1

A.M.F.

My dear daughter,

  1. It is very late, but I do not want to send you the sisters without a letter from me. Listen, one will seem rough to you, but she reads and writes well; the other has a very good spirit and reads and writes well. Listen, if you see that they are not suitable, they will be changed; and if there is time they can be exchanged for those passing through;2 in that case you can also telegraph me, but I hope you will put them in order and will certainly make them useful. For charity's sake, dear Vincenza, because I would have no others.

  2. I have received your letters, but from today's, the last, I see that you have not received mine; I hope they crossed. Listen, they will also have paid you the fare for four sisters, as they had promised me; so on Monday, at the same time you arrived, the sisters will be at Castel Bolognese station; you will wait for them at that station and join them to go to Mercatello.3

  3. At Pesaro you will find the Archpriest, who wrote to me full of courtesies.4 Have him pay the fare too. Listen, for the certificates I shall send you that of Sr. Anna Tecla, who today came back to us,5 and you will withdraw the one belonging to the postulant already at Pesaro; you know whom I mean, the one I sent to Ferrara.6

  4. So see a little: this Archpriest makes so many remarks to me, wanting one with a higher-grade certificate,7 but I hope you will manage; if need be, tell him I shall send one; then withdraw Sr. A. Tecla's for me, and bring me the postulant's too if I have to send one of higher grade. Tell the Archpriest that I deliberately did not send him the other, because first I want to hear whom I should send, one of higher grade or of lower grade.

  1. I have written to the Count and I hope he will be pleased.8 Many greetings to everyone.

  2. When Mercatello is finished you can come back here. For the moment all is going well at Foligno, so you will go there when you have to take the religious for the Duchess; keep silent about it.9

Goodbye, it is too late. Yours on earth and in Heaven affect. M.

She warns her against pride, showing her the spiritual harm it does, and urges her to watch and pray, as Jesus teaches us.

A.M.F.

My dear daughter,

  1. I am writing to you again to let you know that that religious, to explain myself better, the one with the mole, has a petticoat; you will see it; have her take it off; mind you remove the red from it. For pity's sake, tell the superior to keep her under an iron hand; she is very [untaught] and still needs instruction in the Rules and in our life.1

  2. You will have received my letter which I sent you by post; having forgotten to hand it over, I sent it to you by post.2

  3. Do not grow proud on reading your mother's letter because of the praise she gives you. If we have anything good, it is God; we have nothing but wretchedness and sins; we are as ugly as pigs.3 Away with the world and its illusions; only one thing remains for eternity: the good we may do in this life with the help of God the Father; everything else ends up consumed with the earth and lost in the dust and the worms.4

  4. Humility! which we have not yet learned, and it seems that [pride] sprouts in our breast like a worm that is always gnawing; and blessed are those souls who have managed to drive this creature from its nest. Even then they must always labour to stay on guard so that it does not build its nest again, because it is always prowling and its one intention and effort is to achieve its purpose. Alas! [What can we do] but watch, as our master Jesus teaches us: «Watch and pray, if you do not want to fall into temptation»! So, my daughter, let us do it!5

  1. Listen, you know that I have no other treasure than prayer; from it

I have everything, and with it I obtain all my courage; one day we shall find our labours at the throne of God the Judge, and they will defend us from falling headlong into the abyss as we deserve.

Goodbye, greet them all for me, and believe me, on earth and in Heaven, yours more than anyone's

affect. M. Rosa

She has already spoken to him of a young man needing lodging. She is anxious that he be helped, for good reasons.

A.M.F. My Father,

  1. I have received the letter and the box; thank you for everything, and may St Anne repay you; I tell her so every day.1

  2. Listen, I should like a favour, but you must speak to me frankly and as a true friend. You know that little Priest I wrote to you about, who would be coming to take his examinations there;2 I should like to know whether you could lodge him; I would have the Superior in Trastevere give him his meals;3 but you must tell me frankly if it is too much trouble for you; say exactly how you feel. In that case I shall think of turning to others to see whether I can find a room free of charge.

  3. Answer me at once, because it matters to me. You must know that this Priest is a great concern of mine, and when you know the reasons you will say I am right.4

  4. Listen, I seem to hear you say: «The mother is always up to something; she hasn't enough of her own, she goes looking for new ones!» Ah! My Father! The Charity that governs me never says enough; but it can tell you that it is stronger than my strength, since it is in my very depths that it does violence.5

Burn, burn this monster of a letter of mine, and believe me ever your poor

Sister Anna Rosa Gattorno

The Count is not happy with the new Sisters. She agrees to withdraw one and decides that she should go to Mercatello. To Lugo she will send another Sister who will be the new Superior, replacing Sr. A. Edvige, whom she assigns to Mercatello.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Yesterday I received a telegram from the Count telling me that they do not like the two I sent them.1 Listen, [about] one he may be right, but about the other he is wrong.

  2. So the one from Rome must stay, and the one with the mole will serve as cook at Mercatello, and to you there I shall send another with whom they will be pleased, namely Sr. A. Innocenza.2

  3. You will take the Superior, Sr. A. Edvige, with the one with the mole, to Castel Bolognese, and so the Superior3 will take Sr. A. Innocenza and you will take away the one with the mole; the other is to stay. The post is leaving, enough; I am

Affect. M. R.

Further arrangements regarding the Sisters to be assigned to Lugo and Mercatello. She is to urge the Superior at Lugo to keep an eye on the two Sisters arriving and help them become true religious.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. This morning I wrote to you,1 and now again; I hope you receive this in time; meanwhile do this: you will no longer take the Superior with you, but the two they want me to remove,2 and so one of them, the one from Rome, you will send back down alone, because I do not think it good to take her to Mercatello.3

  2. So at that station you will find the two who are to go to Lugo, and you will keep the one with the mole as cook for Mercatello, with Sr. A. Battistina as Superior and Sr. A. Carmelina as teacher, and you will tell them that [for] the other teacher I am waiting to know how I should send her, whether of lower grade, as is the certificate they have, or else they will return me the lower-grade certificate and I shall send them the higher-grade one; tell the Archpriest so.4

  3. If Sr. A. Alberta could be here by Monday morning I should be glad; see what you can do. The two for there will be Sr. A. Innocenza and Sr. A. Stanislaa, who will do their year of training.5

  4. Listen, for charity's sake, tell her to keep them in sight, for charity's sake, and not leave them alone; urge her to watch over them, for they are two girls who need supervision; I add nothing more, because I want to post this.

Yours in haste

Affect. M. Rosa

She gives her opinion about the Vernengo Sisters. She is pleased with how the House is going.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have received your letter; it consoles me greatly to hear the good news of the House, and that you are paying off the bills.1

  1. The answer you gave the Vernengo sister is from God, because it is inspired by Him; you could not have said anything better.2 Firmly: I do not allow them ever to go out alone; as long as they wear the habit they must respect it. That is how it must be done, without pity; in our Rules no exception of any kind is to be made. Let them turn to the major Superiors, who will answer them as is fitting.

  2. For the rest I am pleased and I bless you a thousand times, that it may give you strength and encouragement.

Your Affect. M. R.

P.S. Mind you send me the accounts for the year 1874.

She hopes they will be pleased at Lugo with the two new Sisters. She is to send off the other, who is unsuitable. She tells her that on her return from Mercatello she must go to Lugo for at least two days and then to Foligno.1

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. Just a line, because it is late and I am so busy that you certainly could not believe it. So I hope these two I am sending for Lugo will be liked, and also these three you will take to Mercatello.2 I am waiting for that one on her own whom I told you to send me, who seems half dead. I would have said it would go like this, because I don't like her. Enough, now I have arranged everything and I hope there will be no more trouble.

  2. On your way back you will go to Lugo again and so see whether everything is going well, and you can stay there two days; and then, on your way here, you must go to Foligno; remember that I promised it,3 but I hope you will be quick at Mercatello.

  3. Goodbye for now; the sister will tell you by word of mouth many things that cannot be put in writing. Your affect.

[Mother]

If you run short of money, write to me in time and I shall send you some. I hope you will be here by the end of January. Yours for all ages. Amen, more yours than mine, and I your affect. M.

Motherly advice. He is to beware of bad companions and look for work. He should join the Society of St Vincent and pray to the Lord with trust.

A.M.F. My Alessandro,

  1. I have received your letter and, listen, you certainly cannot imagine how much pain it caused me; I do not allow it and I shall never consent.1 Listen, try to be a good Christian, keep away from bad companions, and go home early.2

  2. For charity's sake, Alessandro, I beg you to leave those companions; when they tell you that I cannot keep you, answer that so far you have been a burden to no one but your mother, and that it will always be so.3

  3. I hope the job will come. Try to go and see Magnini4 often, and you will see that by pestering him you will get it.

  4. Oh! how glad I should be if you gave everyone a slap in the face by enrolling in the Society of St Vincent!5

  5. You must know that I belonged to it for a long time, and you will see that the Lord will grant you the graces you desire.

  6. I have no one in the world but my God; from Him I have and obtain everything; see what graces He continues to give me! Ah! my dear Alessandro, listen, turn to the Lord and you will have everything.6

  7. I await a letter from you telling me that you have enrolled; what a consolation to see my son going to the poor to help them! The consolation would be too great for me! It depends on you. Yours, because it is late, most affect.

M. R.

She asks her to buy and send booklets of the «Crown of the Lord».1

A.M.F.

[Dear daughter,]

  1. I should like you to do me the kindness of buying me 24 Crowns of the Lord.2 You know, the little booklets you sent me once before, which Fasicorno sells near San Matteo.

  2. Put them all together and then, with a piece of paper cut like a band, put it round the middle and with another form a cross, with two (illegible word).3 I hope you will send them soon.

Goodbye, your M.

She advises how to handle a school problem and how to behave with the school Inspector.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I have just received yours with the register enclosed; listen, these threats are of no account for us, because with God's help we do what we can in all conscience.1

  2. To find out where they live, ask the girls themselves, as we do here; only I am writing to you as we have written too.2 For the rest, once you have done it, go to the Inspector, you and the Superior, not the lay teacher, and ask him with humility and gentleness whether it is all right, saying that if it is not right you will do it again, and that he should come and see how the schools are going and whether they please him; that you are not satisfied unless He comes and assures you of it.3

  3. In this way you will be sure of not being in breach, and if he finds anything that is not right you will do it again. Send me news at once of what he told you, because I am anxious.

  4. If I need to send Sr. A. Vincenza I shall send her; it certainly makes me fear there is something behind it, since this one is made differently from those I have received.4 See that nothing happens. Goodbye in haste, your Affect.

M. Rosa

Worried about her health, she urges her to take care of herself. She is waiting for her. Afterwards she must go to Uppello.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I received yours through Sr. A. Alberta,1 and I hear that your voice is still weak. Alas! how I suffer over it, you certainly cannot imagine. If it is true2 that you love me and want to be a comfort to me, take care of yourself, for charity's sake.

  2. I forgot to send you the privileges for the chapel; I am sending them to you at once.3

  3. Take care of yourself; I cannot wait for you to be finished,4 so that you can come and rest, because it is certainly nothing but tiredness.

  4. They are expecting you at Uppello, but keep silent, because you know why.5 Enough, I shall tell you many things by word of mouth.

Your affect. [Mother]

5. Carlottina is in bed with a swollen face and last night she gave us all a bad time. Enough, she is sleeping now and I hope it will be nothing much,

your Affect. M.

Worried by her silence, she asks her to write. She has appointed Sr. A. Carlotta Biagini superior of the Mother House.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I am in a state because I have no letters from you; I do not know what to think; that you are ill, I say to myself: she would have had someone else write; in short, I think all sorts of things.1 Put me out of my anxiety.

  2. I enclose F. 5, which you gave Sr. A. Albertina and which they would not take here, as they are from your part of the country; so try to spend them, and don't keep any, because they are not accepted here.2

  3. Today I made Sr. A. Carlotta Superior here; because, as we must leave when you come, it was certainly not advisable to wait and appoint her when we were on the point of departure.3 I am sure you will be pleased.

  4. Ah! what a sad day! Sr. A. Benedetta did nothing but cry; and I, with my temperament; how painful to see someone cry for no reason. Enough, you will hear by word of mouth what mercy of God it is that allows this for my sins.

Yours in haste affect. M. R.

She has received her first letter. She is to withdraw the certificate that is not needed and send it to her.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. At last I have received yours, which I see is the first you have written me, because you give me the first news of the journey and of the welcome you received.1

  2. Listen, for charity's sake withdraw the teacher's certificate, you know she is now at Ferrara, because it is no longer any use to you, unless I send her; well, we shall see; this is more than the 4th time.2

  3. Believe me, my dear, the work increases beyond measure; I really wish you could [...].3 I must stop, otherwise, you certainly cannot believe it, this letter will never go.4

Your affect. M. R.

She feels the distance and needs help, but finds everything in God. She urges her to love Him. She asks her to look into Alessandro's situation and find out from mamma Adelaide whether it is true that they want to send him to America. She is also to try to speak with Signora Morando.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. You tell me you have no letters from me; what can I do, my dear, I am so busy that I do not know what to do first.1 If you knew

[h]ow this morning, at a moment of certain complications, I wished you were near me. Enough, so God wills; you had spoilt me too much, and I took advantage of your charity and goodness, so now I am paying for it all; there is no longer any danger of my having someone to lean on.

2. But in God I find all I need. He makes up for the emptiness left by creatures. Oh! how good He is to me! Yes, I cannot help telling you with all the strength of my soul: «Love, love God and then you will have everything. The flesh groans under the weight of a prolonged martyrdom in this vale of sorrow and anguish; where does it find its relief? In that infinite Being in whom everything is found, because if the flesh suffers, the spirit rejoices, and so sorrow becomes sweet as honey».2

  1. Listen, if you could go to Genoa for a little to see how Alessandro is, and at the same time call on Mr Magnini, you know, that sick Gentleman we visited together, to see whether he has found anything yet for Alessandro; and also hear a little what Mamma says.

  2. Do you know what they have now got into their heads? To send him to America.3

Tell me, what do you think? How dreadful! Can God want this too? Ah! no, it is not because he is my son according to the flesh, but his soul, which is dearer to me than my own eyes! There, in that abyss of a thousand errors, there where every kind of unbelief is found, in short the beginning of hell for a poor young man who, with no experience of the world, must throw himself into it! Where! Alas!4

  1. Don't let it be noticed that I have spoken to you about it, but hear what she tells you, and then answer her whatever the Holy Mother puts into your mind.

  2. Listen, I have been told in a letter that a man fell from a window in your hospital; is it true?5

  3. Find out what is the matter with Signora Morando;6 I hear she is displeased, and it grieves me to hear she is displeased; if there is something, let her have it written to me and I will put everything right. It would be a serious matter now if she were to take offence.

  4. My God! how many troubles! For charity's sake, see to this at once, don't let days go by, because it could do harm; so I hope you will do it promptly.

Goodbye, yours for ever and ever

Amen affect. M. R.

She speaks to him of a «difficult» young woman he has entrusted to her, assuring him that she will do her best to help her mend her ways.1

Most Rev. Excellency,

  1. I beg your pardon for the mistake of putting someone else's letter in place of Paolina's; it grieved me greatly.2 Only the charitable expressions of your esteemed letter assure me of your indulgence.

  2. As for Paolina,3 Your Most Rev. Excellency may be sure that I shall do as you tell me, but I find in her such duplicity that it worries me a great deal. The kindness shown her is beyond compare, and unfortunately she is indifferent to it. May God hear our prayers and convert her.

  3. I cannot set out certain of her tricks in a letter, but if the good Lord grants me to be at Your Feet, I shall tell you everything freely and Your Most Rev. Excellency will know how to find the means to convert her truly; I am certainly not capable of it, lacking every virtue and all knowledge, a poor little woman with nothing good in her.4

  4. I cannot express to you how grateful I am for your prayers; I need them too much.

Deign to grant me your pastoral blessing while, on my knees, I declare myself with the highest esteem and admiration

Your Most Rev. Excellency's Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

She is glad they have a confessor; she is to tell Fr Accinelli and also ask him to look into the larger house. Advice about the nurses. She asks her to have the Sisters pray for certain intentions of hers.1

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I was glad to hear that the abbot has agreed to hear your confessions. I hope you have mentioned it to Fr Accinelli; so you can go to his Parish quite well, a few at a time, but let us hope that later he himself will say he will come to you. Accinelli must inform the Archbishop, otherwise there will be trouble later; enough, I am writing to him now;1 and I also enclose two lines for you to give to the abbot.

  2. See that Fr Accinelli takes up the matter of the house you say would suit you.2

  3. For charity's sake, try to ensure that the nurses observe the point about not separating; and take care not always to send the same ones to the place where the same four always go. Without changing them, you can split them up by having one lose two nights in a row and sleep during the day; in that way they get somewhat changed round. You understand me, don't you? If you have not understood, write to me and I shall try to explain in another way.3

  4. So I urge you to watch that they are not sluggish with the sick but try to be all charity, that they do not put on airs; in short, try to keep watch, get the most exact reports and contrive to know everything; and seeing you discreet, they will confide in you more and be sure that you will not give them away to the sister accused.4

  1. For two days now I have had a certain fear about your house. For charity's sake, keep a hundred eyes open and watch the young ones closely so that nothing happens;5 in short, my daughter, I hope you will listen to my teachings and put them into practice.

  2. Have prayers said: first, that you may have the house you mention; second, that I may not have to take the oaths; and the other is the grace I am waiting for day after day.6 Oh! certainly, if the nurses did their works of charity well, I would obtain everything.

Goodbye, the Lord bless you and all the Sisters, while I am your

Affect. M. R.

Sr. A. Benigna, formerly Sr. A. Tecla, will arrive at Mercatello; she is to welcome her warmly and commend her to the Superior. Advice on organising the school.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. You will receive this letter of mine from Sr. A. Benigna; she was formerly Sr. A. Tecla, but you will embrace her and give her a thousand welcomes as if she were the dearest of all, and commend her warmly to the Superior;1 and see that you do not hand her certificate over to the Inspector, because I hope to change it soon, as I need it badly.2

  2. Try to keep her cheerful, and if Sr. A. Carmelina comes out with any of her remarks, tell her she must say nothing; she is not allowed to bring anything up again, or to mention the least of the things that happened.

3. The girl is in the fourth class3 and will help very well, and will pass as a postulant studying for her certificate, as indeed she is; do you understand? And you will bring me down the certificate of the lay teacher, the one from Ferrara.4 It seems to me that in this way everything will go well; and you can come down soon, because two days' stay at Lugo will be enough.

4. The girl will stay with Sr. A. Carmelina; meanwhile she will continue her studies, and I want her to learn enough to be able to take her certificate. So try to arrange to bring me down the Postulant's certificate. By word of mouth; we shall see each other soon. Remember that they must pay your fares.

Yours for ever Affect. M.

P.S. Tell Sr. A. Battistina to write to me often.5

She must not complain if she does not write. There is only one reason: her many occupations. She holds her «ever close to the Heart of Jesus». She is to pray and persevere in her good resolutions. She awaits news of the coming audience granted them by the Holy Father.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I have received your letter and hear your complaints at not having letters from me in reply to yours; listen, the reason is my immense workload; I assure you I do not manage to do even the most important things; so when you see me slow to reply, you must think that it is the immense business that prevents me, and nothing else.1

  2. Know that this poor mother of yours always holds you close to the Heart of Jesus, so that one day she may have you with her for an eternity of joy; this is my wealth, this is all I think of giving you.2

  3. Yes, my daughter, if you persevere in your vocation, you will have what I tell you. Yes! I want it! And you assure me of it with the resolutions you have made, which were very pleasing to me to read. So take heart, let us put into practice what we say in words to our Dear Jesus.

  4. Tell the Superior that everything she says in her letter is fine; and so tomorrow, Friday, through you I shall receive the treasure of the Holy Father's Holy blessing; and I await a letter from you telling me in detail what he said to you and how you did, whether well or badly.3 Goodbye, the Lord bless you together with all the others.

your Affect. M. R.

Alessandro is causing her great sorrow. She hopes to see her again soon. She thanks her for the oil she sent.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I have just finished reading your letter and hear about the man; but God permits it so that we may have ever more reason to humble ourselves; enough, let us leave everything to Him.1

  2. Do me the kindness of getting this letter of mine to Alessandro, and take good care not to give him more money than I have allotted him. Oh! the things he does! I assure you they are dreadful, and the more money he has, the more wickedness he commits. And this only feeds his vices. For charity's sake, give him nothing! How bad he is! Ah! it takes the life out of me to think of so many offences against God!2

  3. Let us hope to see each other soon; what can I do, I don't know what to say, I never get anyone I can count on; let us pray the Lord to send me some, and then I assure you I shall send you one.3

  4. I have received the oil, thank you; this blessed House is always in need beyond measure. Whoever is here4 really has cause for worry; one never finds the means to manage to do anything, being always without resources. Goodbye, that is enough for now. I am well.

She is to send off, if she thinks fit, the two Sisters she wrote about. She is to press Fr Accinelli to see to the house to be bought.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. How sorry I am that you keep sending me things; I don't want them, because grass is quite good enough for me.1 I hope you received those rags; but as soon as I can, which I hope will be next week, I shall send you a length of cloth from which you will make plenty of kitchen linen.2

  1. For charity's sake, if you think this sister you suggest sending here is careful, then send her to me at once. I hear there is one from Invorio who is threatening to leave. You can send her to me, so that when her parish priest comes he will take her away.3

  2. For charity's sake, keep after Fr Accinelli to see to the large house you mention. Let him buy it; it will be paid off little by little.4

My daughter,

My daughter,

Alessandro is well and has recovered very well.1 Alessandro absolutely insists that I write asking you to send him some Havana cigars, which cannot be found here and which the doctor has prescribed for him;2 but don't trouble yourself, because when I come we shall send them to him with someone who may have to go back. She sets out the purpose of the Institute and the works of charity it carries out.

[Most Rev. Excellency,]

  1. I was informed by Monsignor our Bishop of Piacenza1 that Your Most Rev. Excellency would like to know what our functions are and whether there might be a certificated teacher to send to one of the villages of Your Most Rev. Excellency's Diocese.2 I am most fortunate to cherish the hope of one day becoming your humble servant, and I take heart to describe to you the functions of our Institute.

  2. The purpose of the Daughters of Saint Anne is the free nursing of the sick of every age, sex and condition, and also the instruction of children of 11 and under. We neither depend on nor are linked to other Religious Houses,3 depending only on the bishops in spiritual matters.

  3. With fewer than three Sisters we cannot accept requests for Houses; four are sent, however, but the fourth remains at our expense, that is, the Institute's and not that of those requesting. We do not usually send the Constitutions; we bring them with us and hand them to the Bishops for them to read and return to us afterwards.

I trust I may become what I profess myself with the highest esteem and respect, asking your apostolic Blessing.

Most humble Most devoted Servant Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

My dear daughter, all mine,

  3. Yesterday it was decided to go to Florence; that excellent Archbishop wants us there for nursing only. What a great House it will be! This news too will please you.5 Enough.

  1. Here I am with you again; yesterday I sent you two letters, and today another chance to write to you comes my way.1 Oh! how gladly I do it, even though I have a very «kind» headache.

  2. Listen, I am anxious, because all my letters will be there, and if by misfortune there were an important one, listen, send them to me at once so they do not get lost, because you know the little devil is really jealous of the Work of Saint Anne.2 If there are any from Sr. A.   1. Just a line to thank everyone for the prayers they offered.   2. And how are you? I am sorry I came, because now I have no peace; I should like to see you;3 there are moments when I suffer not a little. There are people about and I am sorry for it.4 Goodbye, God bless you, your

Affect. M.

Tell the Superior I shall write to her another time5

She invites her to come to her by carriage. She is worried about Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino's health.1

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. For charity's sake don't write to the Superior, because it would do harm; you will hear by word of mouth.2 My God, so many things! I hope you will come soon; take care of yourself.

  2. I don't like the look of Sr. A. Vincenza at all; I fear she will go the way of poor Delaide. This thought is killing me, it gives me no rest.3 More in person.

  3. If you come, try to come by carriage; have it come to your door, and so here to S. Donato.4

Goodbye, your affect. M. R.

She is worried about Alessandro, who she hears is involved with a woman of ill repute and has signed two bills of exchange. She suggests she advise him on the matter. She has been ill with a «frightful bronchitis» and is now up.

A.M.F. My Onorata,

  1. I am writing to you on my knees, with anguish in my soul over certain matters concerning Alessandro which are very painful to me, and which you alone must know, so that you can try to remedy what may happen.

  2. Listen, Acc. insists that while I was in Piacenza Alessandro ran off with that horrid woman and went with her to Genoa, because this wretched creature is always tormenting him and is now plying her ugly... my God!1

  3. You must also know that two bills of exchange have come to light, made out with Alessandro and others.2 Who enjoyed the money they will know, but since Alessandro is under age they cannot touch him at all; only I would not want him to make any written promises. He is out of all danger because, as I tell you, he is not of age; so he must turn a deaf ear to everything and not reply to any of the threats they may make.3 For charity's sake, try to persuade him that they are all rogues; I use this word because if you had heard how they got him to make them, or rather how they made them, it is dreadful.

  4. So, dear Onorata, try to find out everything they have written to him; I fear Alessandro may let himself [be drawn] into something;4 I should also like you to point out to him that he must not squander money, because he is a real bottomless pit of extravagance and will not consider his position at all;5 for charity's sake.

  5. I hope you have received the vegetables; today I am sending you a basket of fish and two of pasta.

  6. Give me news of Sr. A. Vincenza; I find it hard to write and I am alone, so to speak; I had a frightful bronchitis that brought me very low. I am up, but I cough all the time and am extremely weak.

  7. The lawsuit has been heard; now I am awaiting the decision.6 Read this as best you can.

  8. I assure you these affairs of Alessandro's grieve me to the heart. Yesterday one of these bills; I suffered greatly; I hope he does not do anything as foolish as letting the chain and watch go.7 I beg you, he must stand firm and not reply. Yesterday I was advised: if they dare to come, send them away saying he has nothing;8 in this way it will all end. Onorata, I beg you.

Goodbye, yours for ever

Affect. Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

She begs him not to pay the bill of exchange. She has taken advice from competent people. She herself will see to paying off the debt. He is to stand firm and keep to what she has written. If he really disagrees, he is to let her know.1

A.M.F. My Alessandro,

  1. I beg you for the love of God not to get it into your head to pay the bill on the spot;1 I have no money; it would mean taking that very small capital Accinelli holds, which is reduced to the minimum; so I took advice, and was advised not to pay and indeed to stand firm, because this is money that was handled by others, not by you, and since you are not of age they cannot do you the slightest harm.2

  2. Moreover, we have this gentleman's girl boarding with us, which is paid for little by little, because I shall keep her without charging anything; so the Fr. 300 will soon be paid. See, at 20 F. a month, in a year and 4 months it is paid off. Do you think that is all right?3

  3. I am truly in despair, because I do not know where to lay my head; troubles come crowding upon me and I feel I can bear no more. You obey; turn a deaf ear to all the letters and threats, which are worthless, because the law protects you. Since you are not of age, they can do nothing, nothing to you.4 Rest easy; they are all bogeymen.

  4. I have made thorough enquiries; they try everything, they go to your uncles, they come to me, to Accinelli, and knowing they have no power at all, they try every avenue. Alessandro, stand firm, for pity's sake, because you see that this Gentleman will be paid little by little; I do not know where to find the money.

  5. Write to me at once, or rather, tell me whether you are happy with what I have done.5 I have written to Onorata, sending the letter registered.6 I find myself with heavy commitments and do not know how to get out of them. I receive not a penny from anywhere; tell me if you are happy; I thought I was doing right, but if you are not happy, write and tell me and I shall try to do as you wish.7

  6. Goodbye; I write to you in the depths of sorrow, because at this moment other afflictions come to pierce me, and I still cannot manage to sit at the desk; I am writing to you on my knees.8

your most affect. M. R. Gattorno

She categorically forbids her to offer herself to God as a victim for Vincenza's health or her own. She is to take care of herself and get well.1

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. First of all I forbid you to offer yourself to God, whether for Sr. A. Vincenza, or for me,2 or for anyone else; indeed I declare, with all the authority God has given me over the Daughters of Saint Anne and over you in particular, that I do not want your offerings to be heard; on the contrary, under Holy Obedience, ask God's pardon and tell Him that you want to get well and live a hundred years because of the obedience you owe me; so I will it, so be it.3

  2. Stop uttering heresies once and for all;4 be cheerful and you will live. Sr. A. Vincenza is getting better, and I hope the good Lord will restore her to full health; I am better, indeed I am well, and I hope to come and see you. Try to get well and take the decoction; it cured me, I have no more cough, I am well.5 Ah! If Sr. A. Vincenza had had faith and accepted it, she would have been cured.

Your affect. M. R...

She asks for news of Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino's treatment and health.1

My daughter,

  1. I have received your letter. For charity's sake, I hear you are mixing pills and decoction; be very careful what you are doing.2

  2. I should like to know whether the issues look good, whether they are discharging; and also what the sputum is like.3

  3. For charity's sake, don't tire yourself too much on those stairs; call someone, have things carried. Tell Anna, regarding what she put in her letter about paying for her board, I do not want her to talk about it, otherwise she will displease me.4 How is Sr. A. Vincenza? Is she taking the oil?5

Goodbye, yours for ever affect. M. R.

God bless you.

She gives precise orders on how the Sisters are to behave towards Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino and her mother.1

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. Here are my orders. I command and will that none of the religious go into Sr. A. Vincenza's room. I want no one to go in except Sr. A. Santina and Sr. A. Costanza, and no one else. I absolutely do not want the nuns to linger upstairs, none in the little study, not one, for charity's sake;2 and woe to any religious who stops to talk to Signora Rapallino!3

  2. I am tired of gossip; I don't want to hear any more; from the portress to the cook, I insist that they do not talk to outsiders. So these two alone are to nurse Sr. A. Vincenza and no one else. Oh! how much reaches me through the wicked tongues of nuns!4

  3. Send for the bricklayer and have a stove put in Sr. A. Vincenza's room at once, and tell Signora Rapallino that I have no better room for her daughter, because my little study is too small for her, as she suffers from breathlessness.5 So the master builder is to buy one at once and install it; spare no expense. I cannot understand how my little study is also used for recreation and a bit of everything; enough.6 I am not able to come, being too weak.7

I am yours, in haste, your

Affect. M.R.

She tells her that the next day she will receive a letter with a note for Sr. A. Vincenza.1

A.M.F.

Dear daughter,

1. I am letting you know that tomorrow you should receive a letter addressed to you, and inside there is one for Sr. A. Vincenza,2 in which I told her to get well and do the obedience, for I intend her breathlessness to stop at once, as I hope she will be better.

Goodbye, be careful, for charity's sake your affect. M. R.

She suggests how to behave in nursing Sr. A. Vincenza and what to answer those who criticise what she is doing. She is to give the enclosed note to the patient.

A.M.F.

Dear daughter,

  1. I have just received a letter from you and hear what you tell me about Sr. A. Vincenza.1 Yes, courage; I urge you to give her the oil of the Eternal Father, and when she coughs, rub her throat with it if she cannot swallow it, but as soon as she can, a teaspoonful, at once; faith.2

  2. For charity's sake, don't tell anyone about it, as you did with the decoction;3 luckily I hear you have finished it, otherwise I would be anxious. Mixing the decoction with the doctor's medicines, my God! for charity's sake! Enough. I hear she is better; give her these two [lines].4

  3. Laugh at them all, and when she sends for you, laugh and answer her: «What do you want? I am under obedience and must do this; when I receive another order, then I shall carry it out. For now I shall not depart from obedience. Rest assured that I do nothing on my own initiative; and I am sure you will believe me; but if you do not believe me, write to the one down there and you will see whether I am telling the truth».5

  4. Listen, before you leave, ask for four Crucifixes for those here who don't have one; and if you need anything else you can do the same; get them to give you them.

  5. «It is time to get up — you will tell Sr. A. Vincenza — and to do the Obedience».

  6. Greet everyone for me. I am not writing because I am weak; I

urge you to keep the oil hidden.6 Goodbye! Courage, don't trouble yourself, for charity's sake don't wear yourself out.

Your affect. M. R.

7. These two lines for Sr. A. Vincenza: once she has read them, tell her to give them back to you, sealed in another envelope, because you know very well that when making the bed or moving about they might fall out, and woe to anyone who saw them! I rely on you, for charity's sake!

She has heard that Sr. A. Vincenza is better and hopes for steady recovery. She is to try to return to Genoa to free her from her commitments to the community.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. Yesterday, from the telegrams Signora Rapallino sent her husband, I see that the patient is better; so listen, see whether you can come down, because I really need you; leave Sr. A. Costanza there and you come, because otherwise I am too tied,1 and besides there are so many things to do; so see about coming, especially as this week the oaths are to be taken.2

  2. Do everything you can to come as soon as possible; Signora Rapallino, it [seems] to me, will be enough with one nurse, and so you can manage it. I hope Sr. A. Vincenza will not relapse and will go on improving.

  3. I am anxious because I have not received the Father's letter which you say told me everything about Sr. A. Vincenza; tell him it has been lost;3 for charity's sake, be careful how you post them.

Goodbye, greet Sr. A. Vincenza for me and tell her she must obey absolutely.

your affect. M. R.

Advice on her duties as Superior of the House and instructions for two Sisters' journey to Pennabilli.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I have just received your letter in which you say you wrote me another on the 27th; I have not received it and I am anxious,1 because I know nothing of whether you received the Sisters who left for Pennabilli. I cannot understand how letters get lost.2

  2. You tell me that this Lady goes into the kitchen; I am amazed that you have given her such free rein; what, she goes into the kitchen? Alas! for pity's sake I would not want her to meddle in these matters, because when she wants something she must ask for it, not go there. So act as Superior.

  3. Oh! how distressing! For charity's sake, I rely on your good sense to see that she goes nowhere and sees nothing; you know this already without my telling you.3

  4. Listen, you must send to Pennabilli the one from Invorio whom you clothed, who teaches the boys, and her companion; I think I have explained myself clearly. First you will write to the Superior to let her know, and give them the name of the inn; you can also write two lines to this Gentleman asking him kindly to see the sisters safely onto the mail coach and commend them to the driver.4

  5. In short, my daughter, I urge you to do all you can so that everything goes well. I need the superior;5 try to leave Sr. A. Costanza in the house, near Sr. A. Vincenza, so that if another is needed she can choose whichever she finds most alio greeable; but I need Sr. A. Santina, because I am unwell and cannot tire myself.6

6. I am sorry to hear you are upset, but I was obliged to give these warnings;7 be of good heart, for it will all end; I cannot write; see how I tremble from weakness.

Goodbye, the Lord bless you; I am your affect. M. R.

Contrary to what she wrote earlier, she tells her to stay with Sr. A. Vincenza. She is to ask the Father on what day he is leaving for Genoa.

My daughter,

  1. I wrote to you to come.1 Now I tell you to stay, because I hear from Sr. A. Vincenza's brother that she wants you to remain.2

  2. If the Father decides to come, let him telegraph us, because in one letter he tells me he is coming and in another he is not;3 then in yesterday's he says he is coming on Wednesday, and in this one I have just received he says nothing, so I do not know what to think. Write to me, for you know I understand all your letters.4

Goodbye, your affect. M.

She regrets that her letters have not arrived. Others sent from Piacenza have also gone astray. She would fly to her Vincenza and is distressed at being far away, but she cannot: she is very weak. Onorata is to put «bad» thoughts out of her mind. She will never forget her or her family. Alessandro does not write to her.

A.M.F.

Dear Onorata,

  1. I have just received your letter1 and am replying in my own hand; you tell me of letters you wrote to me which I have not received at all;2 indeed yesterday I said: «how can it be that my Onorata doesn't write to me?» And I was anxious about it.

  2. I am up but very weak, so that I find it hard to write because of the stomach pain I have; I assure you that if I had a little strength I would have flown to my Vincenza, but patience! I assure you I cannot describe to you the pain and anxiety I feel at being far from her.

  3. Carlottina cries all the time, she can't put her mind to anything, and she would like to come and see Sr. A. Vincenza, but how? I don't like letting her come alone, because I am afraid.3

  4. Now allow me to give you a just reproof about your supposed ideas, or rather bad thoughts: that I might forget you and your family, and that my affection and gratitude might fail?!!!!.… Examine yourself a little and then see whether that could happen! No, no, it is among the impossible things! Living and dead, I shall always be grateful and affectionate to you!4

  5. I cannot understand how I have lost all the letters which here in

Piacenza they tell me they sent on the 27th, the 26th and the 28th. I have received none of them. What can it be? I cannot understand it. If you knew how much I suffer in writing and how much I have to write, you would certainly pity me.5

6. I enclose F. 20. Together with the fifty you have, give them to our good mamma with my greetings and tell her many, many things from me. Alessandro does not write!! And yet I wrote to him that it was certainly not up to me to write to him. Patience! It is written that I must drink the whole cup of bitterness; may God's will be done for ever!

Yours, yours for all ages

Affect. Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

She asks her to send two Sisters to Genoa and give them some money. She gives various instructions for the house and asks for prayers.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. Listen, first of all don't get it into your head that I am not writing to you; the reason is weakness; I say no more because I really cannot;1 then I want you to send me Sr. A. Albertina and Sr. A. Prassede at once, at once here to Genoa, as I hope you will have sent those for Pennabilli;2 when you send those for Genoa, give them some kitchen linen.

  2. As for wine, buy it, so that what we have will be kept3 for this summer. And if you have collected the F. 500 from the town council, send them to me with the sisters; sew them well into a pocket so that they cannot be seen;4 otherwise, of the F. 500 the Father left you, you can send me 200, if you can, as I have certain expenses to meet for the houses.

  3. Courage, for it is a time to suffer for God. I shall tell you many things by word of mouth.

  4. I hope you will tell me what you are doing about the patient's mattresses and linen;5 and have her room whitewashed and thoroughly cleaned, the tiles too. Listen, as she was not consumptive,6 I would be inclined to have everything washed and then kept for other sick sisters. What do you say?

  5. I would not want anyone to sleep in Carlotta's bed, to spare the poor child distress.

  6. I want you to keep a close eye on Sr. A. Dorotea. You will hear more in person; for charity's sake don't let anything show; she is not to be too much with Sr. A. Virginia, with Sr. A., the one from Nice.7 Goodbye, the Lord bless you together with the Community, and

Believe me your Affect. M.

7. I want you to make a triduum, meaning three rosaries, to the Most Blessed Virgin of Lourdes, lighting candles for her on three evenings, for a benefactress who wants a grace; three evenings the rosary for her; say it aloud.8 Goodbye again, your.

She has been informed, regarding the «Ricchino case», that he demands a further statement. She begs him to advise her how to proceed.

Most Rev. Eminence,

  1. How fortunate I would be if I could fly to your feet for advice; as that is not possible, I ask it in writing.

  2. On the third of this month I was notified of the Ricchino judgement, which obliges me to take 17 oaths, all those concerning religion having been left out, and Mr Tornatore 4; so I must either swear or return the money in full.1 I therefore ask Your Most Rev. Eminence, for the good of the work, what it is best to do.2

Having only fifteen days, deign to reply to me; I am sure of obtaining everything from your immense charity at this moment when tribulations are raining down on me in torrents. A word from you will be a comfort to me. Asking your Pastoral blessing, humbled at your feet, I remain Your Most Rev. Eminence's

Most humble Servant Sr. A. Maria Rosa Gattorno

Regarding the «Ricchino lawsuit», she has been notified that she is called to testify under oath. She awaits his advice before making her decision.

Most Rev. Eminence,

  1. Since I cannot come myself to humble myself at your feet for advice in a most important matter, I must use the pen, sure that by this means too I shall receive the same answer from your immense charity, of which I have had no few proofs.1

  2. Your Eminence knows well that the work of Saint Anne has a lawsuit, and after I have won it several times,2 now, since my opponent can find no other means, it imposes oaths on me: either to swear or to return the money he had given me to open a House seven years ago3 (which still exists), with many girls and nuns, many of the girls having been placed there by that Priest and kept free of charge.

  3. Now I wish to know how I should proceed, as I have only a few days to reply.4

  4. For pity's sake, Your Eminence, do not leave me without an answer, which I await before taking any decision.

Your Pastoral blessing comforts me; may it support me in so many adversities.

Most humble Sr. Anna Rosa Gattorno

A girl placed in the Institute by the «Province» has been wrongly sent away. She regrets it and suggests how to put it right.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I am extremely sorry about what has happened with the girl from the Province, when I had told you not to send away any of the Province's girls, because we could not, you know that; so how did it happen?1

  2. So take her back at once, go to the Prefect and tell him it was a mistake, as it was thought she had been placed by other people, the registers not having been checked at all and memory relied on.2

  3. «She is certainly extremely bad, but we are taking her back, and if after this trial she does not change we shall inform Your Excellency so that you may think of placing her elsewhere».

  4. Meanwhile have her taken at once to the Morte,3 and then the Father will tell you more in person.4

  5. Go at once to the Prefect, fetch the girl at once and take her to the Morte; as for the teacher, leave her free.5 For charity's sake, before sending girls away, think about what you are doing so as not to get into a mess.

  6. You know I have always told you about the Province's girls: we cannot touch them or send them away without a serious reason and without informing the Commission.

Goodbye for now; take courage, don't worry; your affect. M. R. P.S. Before sending any girls away, let me know.

dalla

The Inspector wishes to take a girl from the Institute into service in his home. She tells her which one to send and how to handle it. Some postulants will be arriving. She asks her to clothe the suitable postulants.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I have just received another letter in which I hear that the Inspector wants an older girl for service; for this we must make the sacrifice of giving him one. Listen, you know that when we spoke of this matter we had agreed to give him Rosina; I think she is the strong one who taught at the Morte, and she would go willingly.

  2. Tell this lady that it is being done for her,1 but that it would not have been done for anyone else, as she is a girl we need; but for them we would do anything; and if she does not suit, we shall take her back.2

  3. Then give the girl plenty of good advice;3 tell her to come and see you often and to behave well; in short, that if she is good she may come back whenever she no longer wants to stay there; that will encourage her. I hope you received my letter of yesterday in which I spoke to you at length about the Prefect.4

  4. I want you to clothe all the postulants, meaning those you think are really suited to be clothed;5 one I should like to be the one from Bologna, as I need her. Clothe them at once. Aprotozina;6 you understand me without my explaining further.

Goodbye for now, your affect. M. R.

1. I received your esteemed letter and, to my great regret, did not have the good fortune to be in Piacenza when the excellent Priest went there to agree on the negotiations for a house in your Diocese.2 I am therefore writing to this Curate,3 that if he wishes to come to an arrangement we can use the pen just as well as speaking in person.

2. I therefore warmly thank Your Most Rev. Excellency for having deigned to admit us to the number of your flock, unworthy as we are to be so.

Deign to grant me your Pastoral Blessing as, full of devotion, I declare myself

Most humble Servant Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

  3. Please let me know the number of Religious, also the grade of the teacher,3 and the stipend. On receiving this I shall do all I can to satisfy you.

1. Just a line, although I am weighed down with work. Listen, now is the moment to show me by deeds what you have always told me in words and in writing: the love you bear both me and the Institute. So you must make the sacrifice of staying at the Parrocchietta and, for this year, not coming to Piacenza.1

  1. By October, God willing, I shall be in your arms to stay a good while; so, my daughter, answer me at once to console me and tell me that you are my beloved daughter who wants to be submissive and obedient in everything.2

  2. Receive this letter of mine cheerfully; I shall judge of that from your reply, which I await with the greatest longing. God bless you, I implore it with all my soul, while I tell you I am weighed down with work and so can go on no longer.

Being separated from her costs her not a little. She begs her to take care of herself and write with news of her health.

I A.M.F.

Dear daughter,

  1. Just a line to show you that I am on my feet. Dear daughter, being separated from you costs me not a little.1 Alas! Take care of yourself, for pity's sake, for my only consolation is to hear that you are well; I can bear no more wounds.2 Have pity on one whom I know you love and who returns your affection beyond measure, your Affect. Mother.

  2. Write to me, otherwise I shall be anxious. Did the trip to Genoa do you harm? Tell me the truth, do you understand?3 Oh! how many things I would have to tell you. Oh! where am I? I no longer seem to belong to this earth.4 Dear daughter, I greet you and hold you close to me, as I am your

Most Rev. Excellency,

  1. I reply to your esteemed letter, which I received just now, on the 20th of this month.1 First of all I must say that I am exceedingly ashamed not to have written to Your Most Rev. Excellency before now to thank you for all the care and attention you give to the poor Daughters of Saint Anne. My incapacity cannot express how much gratitude I feel towards so great a benefactor. God will repay you.

  2. As for the House, I am ready to make some small sacrifice, and I would make it more generously if I could have a single line from the Cardinal letting me know that it is his wish that the Daughters of Saint Anne should occupy those premises.2

  4. And also if a blessing of the Holy Father could be had; for the rest, being sure of obtaining what I put to you, go ahead and secure the house, for I am writing now to the Superior in Trastevere to inform her of everything.3

  5. If my health had not tied me down, I would certainly have come to Rome before now, but this year I shall certainly not be able to come. Bless me, while full of veneration I remain, Most Rev. Monsignor, your

My dear daughter,

Send me by Francesco2 the names of the three girls who are to go to hospital, which you forgot to copy out for me last night: one is that little one with scrofula, the other the one who was at the Morte, and the other the one called Tisin. She has received her letters. She will soon have to go to Genoa and will tell her of the «sorrows of the Work of Saint Anne». So she merely gives some urgent instructions about a girl and the postulants.

My daughter,

  1. I have received your two letters.1 Ah! dear daughter, how many sorrows there are in the work of Saint Anne! Enough, everything by word of mouth, because from what I hear from Accinelli I shall certainly not be long;2 be prepared to hear some fine things such as you have certainly never heard yet.

your affect. M.R.

Instructions about the Vernengo Sisters, who want to leave the Institute, and about the girl Paolina.

My daughter,

  1. I have received your letter and telegraphed you at once; now I repeat by letter: do not let the Vernengo sisters go out dressed as Religious even for half an hour unless they have first spoken to Fr Accinelli, whom I have also telegraphed to come and hear how matters stand.1

Affect. M. R.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. Send this letter at once and see: the Vernengo ladies want to leave, but in the habit of Saint Anne, and I would be very sorry about that. I have telegraphed Fr Accinelli and the Superior of the house; how she wanted... my God, how dreadful!2

M. R. Gattorno

She tells him of the illness and death of Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino. A short biography of her will be compiled as soon as possible.

A.M.F. My Father,

  1. A line in my own hand in reply to yours, which was most welcome. God gave me a Creature after His own Heart and all zeal for His Work; He has taken her from me; fiat.1

  2. She died a saint, as she lived virtuously; her illness was a continual sleep of paradise, mysterious even to the doctors; her death a most gentle sleep, wholly absorbed in the most blessed Virgin.2

  4. My Father, I shall not write at length, because I have no small stomach ache; may all the suffering of this poor servant of His be for my God. I am your

Humble Devoted Servant Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

She has received his letter and is grateful for his warnings and advice about Carlotta. She gives explanations and will explain more fully in person.

My Most Rev. Father,

  1. Yesterday I received your esteemed letter, which I read with real pleasure. How could you doubt, my Father, that I might be annoyed by a warning from you? Ah, no! on the contrary, I am most grateful and thank Your Paternity for so charitably giving me good advice.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Just a line, because I am so busy that I don't know which way to turn. Listen, you tell me you have brought up blood again;1 well, I would suggest that you see whether there is still time before the oaths; if so you could ask for 8 [days'] leave and come and stay with me, and then we shall go back to Genoa together, so you could have a little rest.2

So go to the parish priest and beg him earnestly to accept; when he has accepted, go to the Archbishop and tell him. I can't wait to embrace you. Goodbye; come

your affect. M.R.

She answers her question about the price of eggs.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Yesterday I received yours,1 in which you ask me to tell you how much eggs cost; at the last market, last Saturday, the price was 5 centimes an egg; in fact I bought thirty and gave her a little less, four and a half centimes each, and if one buys more they would come even cheaper.   2. I hope you received my letter in which I told you many things;2 as for the Vernengo sisters, you did well to advise her so.3 I can't wait to see you; I hope you will come and spend the feast days with me here in Piacenza.

She tells him the date of a novice's death. Regarding the warnings about Carlotta, she reports the opinion of people she has consulted. She will speak to him about the matter in person.

Most Rev. Father,

  1. Yesterday I received your esteemed letter, in which I found a just complaint against me. It is quite true that I have been negligent.1 My God! what an abyss of imperfections I am... The mass of my occupations keeps me from fulfilling my most heartfelt duties.

  2. So, on 30 April at 5 p.m. the very dear soul of Sister A. Evangelista flew to heaven.2

  3. My Father, now allow me to tell you quite frankly what I told the excellent Marquis Landi when he spoke to me about Sister A. Evangelista. I told him these exact words: I wanted to send her away, and I made representations to Father Santi, who was the one who placed her; but as I am under so many obligations to this Father, I could not help giving in and keeping her, because it is quite true that when they fall ill in the year of novitiate we send them away, but out of regard for Father Santi, to whom I am so indebted, I kept her. Do let the Marchioness3 read these words of mine and you will see whether it is true or not.

  4. Listen, my Father, in these days I have tried asking people of high standing whether what my daughter was doing could give scandal.4 They answered that no one had ever said anything, and that everyone was quite convinced that the poor, unfortunate girl should be able to have a little distraction.

  5. I mentioned the people she goes about with: excellent, they told me. My Father, as for the dinner with the Counts Marazzani,5 this is a downright lie: the girls came one day and stayed until late, and Carlottina let them share the frugal meal, if it can be called a dinner. I really took no notice [of] this nonsense; what do you say?

  1. Listen, my Father, since you give me such freedom to speak, you see, in Piacenza there are a great many people who have never done anything for our poor Institute! I shall tell you the rest in person; only Marquis Alfonso, he indeed has always given and helped me; the others of the family, nothing.

Most humble Servant Sr. Anna Rosa Gattorno

She sends her the letter to be handed to the Superior, Elisabetta, and repeats the invitation to come to Piacenza.

My daughter,

Give this letter of mine to Sr. A. Elisabetta at once;1 I hope to see you soon

your most Affect. M. R.

My daughter,

  2. And don't you fret; be of good heart and do everything for God; a brief suffering is little for an eternity of joy.3

Your affect. M., who wishes you a thousand blessings from Heaven, while I am your affect. M. R.

  1. I received yours with the money order for F 20 and at once sent to the market for the eggs, which are already on their way; I enclose the dispatch note.1

  2. I hear about your troubles and am very sorry, but listen, remember that they are trifles that vanish with an hour's calm.

  3. You will have received my note; stand firm with everyone, for I shall soon be there, as is true, because every day I am waiting to be called;2 tell no one that I am in Piacenza, and if they ask you, say you know I was due to leave. You told me a basket was coming; for your information, we have received nothing; and I tell you not to send any more vegetables, because now there are plenty in Piacenza and there is a risk that I won't even eat them, as there are so many that the community eats them too. Goodbye. In haste, your

She is pleased with the good news of the house. When the beds have arrived, in agreement with the Superior and the Duchess, they can go to Oppello to put the house in order.1

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I am delighted with the good news you give me of the house there;2 God be blessed. Learn from this angel of a Superior, and one day you will be glad of it.3

  2. Everything you answered the Duchess is fine;4 send me the money you have by the Sister who is to come here.5 For pity's sake, let her not lose it. Make yourself all things to all, and especially to those jewels, the dear sick.

  3. Courage; when the beds have arrived you can go to Oppello6 for a few days to set them up, provided the Superior and the Duchess think it right; there are six instead of 5.7 There is a hard mattress; it will do for one of our poor girls; and the bolsters too, if you find them too hard for yourselves, God will provide. Goodbye. Courage, the Lord bless you, and believe me ever your

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. Listen, as for Sr. A. Colomba, take her aside and tell her that if she does not change you have orders to send her away at once and take the habit from her. Meanwhile don't let her out of your sight, for charity's sake.1

  2. Listen, send me Sr. A. Emanuela on Monday the 17th; she can come alone. Listen, with the Fr. 150 you have from the Friar, buy me 18, eighteen weights of pasta with saffron of all the usual kinds; no, or at least very little, a few kilograms (tell Fr Accinelli); a few weights of plain pasta without saffron.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. You will receive this letter of mine from the Sisters I am sending to the hospital; I want to know how many Sisters you are in the Genoa House, with first names, surnames and the number set out in detail; you can get Sr. A. Colomba to give it to you.

I also want to know whether you have collected the money for the stockings we sent the merchant2 and whether he is sending me the cotton, as we have none left; there will be four or five more pairs of stockings which I shall send him at the first opportunity, and also whether he is sending the cotton, as I hope.

A word of advice before she leaves for Piacenza.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

I hear you are not very well; for charity's sake take care of yourself. Listen, bring Paolina with you;1 do me this kindness

your affect. M.

She has had to go to Rome. She had a good journey and is fairly well.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Only just in Rome, since last night; I don't know, this year the good Lord is testing us.1 Oh! my dear, enough; in person, when it pleases God. Meanwhile I have had a good journey and am on my feet, fairly well. Try to take care of yourself, for there is need.2 Goodbye, because I am in a hurry

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I have not written again because of all the work I have; you know, I am writing to you now while I am listening to the sisters.1 Don't worry, I am well; I want you to tell me the truth about yourself, whether you are well or not.2 Try to get strong, for when I arrive I hope to have found someone to relieve you.3

  2. Oh! how much I have to tell you.4 Fr Accinelli telegraphed me about accepting a house with a hospital. I am writing to him now; I would need a hundred arms to do everything that is needed. A.M.F. My Francesca,

  1. I should like you to go to, or call, the superior of the House and tell her to keep Paolina1 until I am back in Piacenza. She is to make her promises and take good care she doesn't run away, for charity's sake.

  2. I hope to be back soon; I shall leave Rome on Monday 31 May and hope to be quick at Terricciola, or rather S. Cassiano.2

  3. I am anxious because I have no news of you; for charity's sake take care of yourself and try not to tire yourself.3 I am well; I commend this business of Paolina to you. Goodbye, because I am very busy, and I hope to tell you everything in person

My dear Count,

  1. I have only just stopped travelling, for in eight days I have not stopped at all,1 and I could not answer your esteemed letter, which I received with such pleasure, all the more as it contained such good news, and the copy of the Holy Father's letter.

  2. My dear Count, what can this poor woman do for you, who do so much good to the Daughters of Saint Anne?2 My God will do it for me, and I shall certainly see my protector and benefactor happy in all his desires.

  3. My dear Count, forgive the poor handwriting and the brevity, but it is time I lack. If God gives me strength, after Saint Anne's day I hope to come to Lugo and thank you better in person; meanwhile please give my greetings to the C.ss your Mother,3 and accept the sentiments of esteem and respect of one who signs herself, of Your IH. The teacher will arrive soon; she must guide her well. She is to ask advice of Sr. A. Domenica, who knows the place.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Yesterday I received your letter and am sorry to hear your complaints;1 be patient, for by the 18th you will have the teacher; mind, she is young and one needs fifty eyes; for the rest I want you always to hold fast to Sr. A. Domenica's advice.2 Listen, she is long in the vocation and so can give you good counsel and teach you what is certainly new to you.

  2. Yes, my daughter, remember that humility is the foundation of every virtue, and whoever has it possesses God.3 Yes, my daughter, learn this beautiful practice and you will have everything from the Lord. Your house will be a jewel in the eyes of my Crucified One, and you will be His Beloved.

  3. Courage, then, for violence is needed to win the kingdom of Heaven.4 I am glad to hear that providence is coming, a good sign; may God pour out His mercy on the whole house.5 Goodbye, all affect.

M. R. G.

Advice on guiding the community well.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I have just received your letter and hear what you have done with the girls;1 you have done well in everything. As for Irene, don't worry, I have already written to her,2 and besides it is only for a short time, because she must then come and take the other examinations in the holidays. You want one long in the vocation;3 I shall send you one when the sisters who are coming to make their vows go back.4

  2. For pity's sake, observance and the timetable, and the practices of piety too: once these are reduced, everything is gone, nothing good remains; the loss of vocation is certain.

  3. So take courage, all for Jesus, life and soul, all for Him. I shall gladly join you in receiving the Holy Father's Holy Blessing. Goodbye, your

She consoles her and promises that at the end of the school year she will go to Piacenza to collect her certificate.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I have received your little letter, which consoled me not a little, hearing that you want to be good and console this poor mother of yours; and she wants to console her daughter.1

  2. Well, listen, be patient and be good, and when the school year is over ask Mgr. Negrotto for permission to come and collect your certificate and, if necessary, take the other examination, so that you could have the higher-grade certificate;2 I shall also write to Monsignor3 asking him to grant you this permission.

  3. Are you happy, my Coca?4 Good girl! So love Jesus, the only aim of our life!5

God bless you; I am your affect. M.R.

She thanks her for her enquiry and informs her about the charitable works of the Daughters of Saint Anne and the practices of the Institute.1

[Most Illustrious Lady,]

  1. I reply at once to your esteemed letter, just received,1 and intend to satisfy you in everything you wish. Allow me first of all to express what I feel for Your Excellency: although I do not have the honour of knowing you, the thought that you deigned to turn your charitable gaze upon us poor Daughters of Saint Anne is enough to make me feel the liveliest gratitude towards Your Excellency; at the feet of my Crucifix, an affectionate prayer for one so kind to us poor creatures.2

  2. Meanwhile I am writing out for you what you wish to know about our Institute. As I cannot send you our Constitutions because of the prohibition we have, with the sole exception of the Bishops — they cannot be given even to confessors —,3 I shall give you fuller information.

  3. Here is the outline. The Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne has as its principal aim among its functions the nursing of the sick of both sexes and every condition, poor and rich, in their homes, free of charge, even in time of any epidemic, without accepting in the sick person's house so much as a drop of coffee or a glass of iced water.

  4. Anyone wishing to give alms, however, must send them to the house addressed to the Superior, because the Sisters must not know that they have been rewarded, so that no spirit of favouritism may enter in. The Superior then receives them as alms and has prayers said for the benefactor; and likewise care and nursing in hospitals.

  5. To take in poor girls who are abandoned and left to

their own devices, keeping them according to their condition.

  1. Also to teach school to poor little boys from 7 to 12 years of age and catechism in the Parish. This is what is usually given to everyone in general.

  2. To you I add this further paragraph. In nursing the sick at home, the sisters always go in twos. In the street they keep silence when passing through inhabited places and occupy themselves with good thoughts. They do not stop in the street with anyone, and if they must give an answer they do so in a few words without stopping. On reaching the sick person's house they at once ask to be shown into the sickroom. In the sick person's house they do every kind of service, from the lowliest to dressing wounds, being already trained by the school held in the Institute.4

  3. There are others who pull teeth,5 and do other surgical dressings, as they already do in many cities. If Your Excellency would like further information, please write to me. As for the financial side,6 provided there is the house and the little we need to live on, we are always content.

  4. Accept, most worthy Countess, my feelings of gratitude, with the hope of expressing our thanks better in person. While I have the honour of signing myself

Your humble Servant Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

Her letters are a comfort, except the last, with its news of poor health. She orders her to take care of herself: her life belongs to God.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I have received your two letters; one was enclosed with dear Edvige's,1 whom I ask you to thank and tell many things from me, for I feel an ever greater affection for her.

  2. My beloved daughter, you will certainly be thinking all sorts of things because I have not written to you again; well, if you were here these days and saw what is happening to me, you certainly wouldn't breathe a word!

  3. Oh! how I long for you, my daughter! Your letters are a real consolation to me, except today's, which tears me apart as I think of you wearing yourself out to the point of having convulsions.2

  4. Alas! for pity's sake take care of yourself; remember that this Mother of yours orders it and wills that her Sr. A. Benedetta take care of herself; remember too that your God is your master, whose slave you have made yourself; you are no longer your own mistress; remember that you belong to God and not to the world. God loves you! Enough, enough, I say no more; God loves you, one day you will see it! Yours in haste,

affect. M. R. G.

She may transfer the Sister from the Genoa house to her community, but only after explaining the reasons to Fr Accinelli.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I received yours today and reply with two lines in haste.1 Listen, by all means take the sister and tell Fr Accinelli why, so that he will be patient, since those who are to make their vows have to come here.2

  2. So mind you don't upset Fr Accinelli, because if you go about it nicely he will say nothing. Take whichever you want, and if you think it best not to send those sisters for their vows, they will come another year. If it were possible it would be good, because you understand me, don't you?3

Goodbye, yours for ever,

M. Sr. A. R.

She cannot wait to have her with her; she has so many things to tell her. She is to think of her Mother, who loves her dearly, and reflect on what she says to her.

A.M.F.

My beloved daughter,

  1. I have just finished reading your dear letter;1 I am stealing a little time to say a word to you in haste, because, without my telling you, I see you already imagine it.

  2. Oh! how I long for you; but Thursday will come soon,2 and then you will be with me; I hope you won't delay any longer, will you? You will hear so many things.
