affect. M. R. Gattorno

There is no need to hasten Sr. A. Benedetta's departure from Genoa; it is better that she come with her. She is waiting to tell her many things.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I have received a letter from Sr. A. Benedetta in which she tells me you advised her to come here; my God! I have telegraphed her not to come, but to come with you. I have nothing outstanding, that is, I manage everything1 very well with God's help; so you see, you know frankly how things are, and I tell you without any veil.2

  2. Oh! I can't wait to talk to you and see you; everything in person. Come, and bring me a little decoction. I have no cough at all now, only a great heat; tell Signora Maddalena.3

Goodbye in haste, your affect. M. R. for ever

She is expecting her together with two Sisters. She is to have the decoction for herself and the Father and two lengths of woollen cloth sent as soon as possible.

Good and blessed daughter,

  1. Listen, you complain that I don't write you everything; and how can I? I would need a thousand legs and a hundred arms;1 in any case I always try to find time for you.

  2. I telegraphed you, and I thought it right to do so. If you come later you will be able to stay longer for Saint Anne's; so on Friday or Saturday, together with Sr. A. Perpetua and Francesca, I hope you will come without fail,2 and you will see that all will go well; and I am sure your papa is so reasonable that he himself will see that on this occasion you must be here.3

  3. Listen, my daughter, I should like you to send me some decoction as soon as possible, both for me and for the Father. As for the cough, tell Signora Maddalena I have none now, only a loss of appetite and a strong heat I feel inside; let her send it at once, and don't forget the Father's; he too feels his stomach upset, for her information;4 but I am on my feet and have time for everything.

Postulants keep arriving; one came who is so refined, from a good family, that I am sure you would like her if you saw her; not for her refined manners, no, no, but because I have high hopes of her for her goodness and good sense. M.R.

7. Remember that you belong to God and so are mine for ever. God bless you, and I am M. R.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

She complains without reason, for she is the only one to whom she writes every day. She gives some news of the house and of Carlotta. She is expecting her with Sr. A. Perpetua.

A.M.F.

My dearest daughter,

  1. Here I am with you again; how it grieves me that you could think you are indifferent to me.1 Ah! this is a real temptation; my reason for making you delay was this: that if you came too early you could not be here for Saint Anne's, which would grieve me too much;2 so if you come on Thursday evening with Sr. A. Imagine how it made me laugh; he already regards her as his [...] (illegible word). If I had had a minute I would have flown to Ferrara.

  4. Goodbye, dear daughter; you certainly cannot believe that I have not a moment to breathe; yesterday when I received your telegram it was too late, since you know very well how often they do things; so it was better this way. Goodbye, your affect. affect. Mother, who always holds you close to her. Ah! yes! you don't believe it; one day you will see it.

Your affect. M.; in Heaven always united for an eternity.

She has assigned two Sisters to her community and commends one of them in particular. She asks for the decoction for the Father and herself.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. Goodbye, I am in a hurry, your affect. M.

My daughter,

ì My daughter,

  1. I received your letter1 and hear what you tell me about the poor girls who failed, of whom we still have a shadow of hope.2 My God! If the Saint granted this grace, it would be a fine thing! Enough, let us leave everything to God. I hear about Sr. A. Benigna.3

Advice on running the Community. She urges her to practise humility, observance and edifying conduct.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I read in your letter what you say about accepting a watch to carry1 from the Capuchin Father; it is not allowed. If it were one of those to hang up in the community, that would not be so bad, but personal ones no, no.

  2. You tell me about Monsignor coming to dinner. If he were really alone, yes; otherwise no, no;2 it is not allowed, because, you see, observance is no longer kept; alas! once one point is neglected, all the others go like a house of cards, falling on top of one another.3

  3. Be firm, observant and docile, without pride: pride is the ruin of all the good of the Daughters of Saint Anne.4 Whoever stays humble is sure to persevere; otherwise it is hard to attain eternal life.5 Always the same with everyone; cheerful, yes, but not with outsiders.

  4. Do not go and eat at the homes of the vine-growers,6 because it is against our Rule; if they want to give you something, accept it and take it home, but do not eat with them.

  5. I hope you already have Sr. A. Panasia with you;7 she will get a little fresh air and some rest, and will also be able to teach the sisters.

  6. Please don't do things that set people talking, for everyone has their eyes on you; so edify your neighbour and give no scandal, I beg you.8

Greet them all for me; I wish them a thousand blessings and they promise me to do well. Goodbye affect. M. R.

She answers her letter at once to reassure her. Her affection for her has never failed. She is to take heart, for she will soon be with her. She is to ask the Director for leave to be away for a few days. She must take care of herself, for the love of God!

A.M.F.

My daughter for ever,

  1. I have just finished reading yours and, instead of going to table, I flew straight to my little study to answer you.1 My dear, how can you possibly think that this mother of yours has fallen short by a hair's breadth in the affection she always has had and has for you? Ah, no, no! That would be barbarous. Ah! You are the only one who enjoys my confidence.2 On earth, among my daughters, I have only you. I say what I used to say to our dear Sr. A. Vincenza: no one will ever take your place, never, never!

  2. Now I have only my Francesca. God keeps her far from me, but soon I shall have her near.3 Oh! that creature without f... will adapt.4 Enough, in person. I count the days and hours, but with all the work I have I tell you they fly by.

  3. I am alone and have had a great deal of work, and I really don't know how to get through it. Listen, today is Monday and I am still alone; you well know how extensive my correspondence is, and yet I do it all; with difficulty, yes, but God gives me life, not health, but life. Oh! dear Jesus, how good You are!

  4. Don't worry that Sr. A. Benedetta has not yet written me anything,5 because she is always unwell. Listen, now I have a plan for you, so that I would not take Sr. A. Benedetta: it would be for you to take a few days' holiday, telling the director that there is a trip to be made to Lake Maggiore,6 which you would gladly make to get away from so many things for a while; and that if He grants it, you will ask the Mother. Hear what he says, then write and tell me.

5. Be cheerful, for when we see each other we shall empty the bag. Goodbye, I am going to dinner; my head is spinning; I still have a regiment7 to write. Yours for an eternity.

6. P.S. Take care of yourself, for the love of God! How painful to hear that you are ill!8 Goodbye.

The Superior has told her of his and the Ladies of the Pious Union's dissatisfaction with the Sisters' work. She has informed the President, the Marchioness Cavalletti. She asks him to tell her what displeases him in the Sisters' conduct. She will try to remedy it after receiving the Marchioness's reply.

Rev. Canon,

  1. I am extremely sorry to have to write you things that are far from consoling. I hear from my poor Superior, Sr. A. Domenica, that Your Reverence and the most Honourable Ladies who support the Institution of Poor Servant Girls are dissatisfied with our work.1

  2. I have informed the dearest Marchioness Cavalletti, most worthy President, of everything;2 I have already told her what I would need to put an end to such unpleasantness, pointing out also that for a good two years the poor Daughters of Saint Anne have served this Pious Union free of charge, without ever receiving the least subsidy, glad to be able to work for so dear and great a protectress of ours; and that they will never manage to do all that is our duty.

  3. Very Rev. Canon, if Your Reverence had deigned, and would deign, to send me what you dislike in the actions of these Sisters of mine, I would not have delayed, nor would I delay, in remedying it.3 Unless Your Reverence intends to put in better educators than the Daughters of Saint Anne.

  4. Meanwhile I can decide nothing until I have a reply from the President, my dearest Marchioness Cavalletti. Please accept the respects of your humble Servant, while I have the honour to remain Your Reverence's

Sr. Anna Rosa Gattorno

The Ladies of the «Pious Union» have accused the Sisters before Cardinal Patrizi of not giving the girls enough food. She suggests that the Marchioness clear up the matter with him. She awaits her decisions to know how to act.

Most Illustrious Marchioness,

  1. I have received your very dear letter.1 God bless you and all your dear family, and accept my good wishes; you will certainly have all your desires fulfilled.

  2. So, since you are so charitable towards the oppressed and allow me to pour out my heart to you, I shall do so frankly.

  3. It is truly dreadful2 to see that those Ladies went and accused us before Cardinal Patrizi as creatures who steal bread from the poor, and made strong complaints that I had put too many religious in that wretched house;3 and so the Superior answered the Vicar: «The Marchioness Cavalletti knew everything; it is on her that we depend».

  4. The Cardinal answered her: «The Marchioness is too charitable, and so she lets everyone do as they please». How dreadful!...4 he said they gave little to eat there; let them do the sums with one franc a day and they will see. Oh! before, they were all for economy; with one franc we are to keep the girls like princesses.5

  1. My dear Marchioness, for pity's sake! Clear this matter up before the Cardinal: we have never had any payment, and you know what toil that house costs us, and all that was done and suffered;6 now this is the reward: they go about slandering us before our Superiors.

  2. I think I have already written to you that I have withdrawn all the nurses and left only 3;7 but that is not enough; I enclose my resignation.8 When you present yours, present mine too; I serve and shall serve you; the others, no, no.

  1. If you want to place servant girls, you can put them at the Lungara where we are; that is your house and mine.9

  2. You withdraw, and I at once want the sisters to leave; what they have done to me is too much: without warning either me or you, they go to the Superiors with such barbarous accusations after we have served them for two years and three months without pay.10

  3. I am writing to the Cardinal now; for pity's sake, plead my cause. Yes! dear Marchioness, may God reward you for all the charity you do; all this has happened because the Cardinal listened to the tittle-tattle and gossip of a wretched servant.

  1. As for accepting that set of rules (if you return as President), I am sure you yourself will see that it cannot be admitted.11 Enough, I shall do whatever you tell me to do, and say in my name to the Ladies whatever you think fit; I always approve and shall approve whatever you say.

  2. Please refute the slanders before Cardinal Patrizi. Forgive me; and kindly give my many greetings to the Marquis your husband and your children. Believe me yours for ever, poor indeed, but most affectionate in Jesus

Sr. Anna Rosa Gattorno

[Most Rev. Eminence,]

  1. I take this opportunity, as the Superior of S. Martinello1 is coming to receive your Pastoral Blessing before reopening the schools, to ask Your Most Rev. Eminence a favour, which I am sure of obtaining from your proven and unequalled charity towards us poor Daughters of Saint Anne.

  2. I would need a Dimissorial letter2 to present to the Sacred Congregation, so that it may be informed of the progress of this poor Institute, and thereby to facilitate its definitive approval. Most Rev. Eminence, deign to include a word that will be effective in achieving the much desired end.

  3. The power and influence Your Most Rev. Eminence has with this Congregation will ensure that at a single word from you the poor Daughters of Saint Anne will be considered and numbered among the chosen ones of the Church.3

  4. God knows how much this most wretched servant of yours longs to come to your feet and tell you in person what she is compelled to do in writing, forced by her poor health.

  5. May my good God therefore interpret all that this most unworthy creature would like to say to you, who have always shown kindness to the poor Daughters of Saint Anne.

  6. Sure of your fatherly protection, deeply humbled at your feet, I implore your Pastoral Blessing, while with all veneration I remain

Your most humble and devoted Servant Sr. Anna Rosa Gattorno

She is willing to take on the service at the hospital in Albano and sets out some preliminary conditions.1

[Dear Marchioness,]

  1. I am replying to your esteemed letter in which you invite me to take on a small hospital; I am ready; only allow me some small remarks: namely, to see that the man is paid by the Congregation or the Town Council,2 since one must reckon not on two sisters but on four, and these are needed if they are to attract3 the sick by giving them good service: so one cook, another in the linen room and at the door, and two nurses, night and day. I hope the hospital's wood will be used for firewood, won't it? as is done elsewhere.

  2. If you obtain this, write to me and I shall send you the Sisters at once.4 Allow me to thank you and express my gratitude, which will be eternal.

Hoping to thank you better in person, I remain, dear Marchioness,

Your most humble Servant Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

She is glad to accept a new work in his Diocese. She thanks him and expresses gratitude for his letter of recommendation.

Most Rev. Excellency,

  1. Through the Superior at Terricciola, by order of Your Most Rev. Excellency, I am asked to accept a house in your Diocese.1 I am delighted to be able to accept it; thus, under your fatherly protection, I shall have the good fortune of seeing a new band of Daughters of Saint Anne added.

  2. As for the Teacher, I hope she will have all the qualifications desired.2

  3. Now allow me to express to you with the liveliest feeling of my heart the gratitude I feel for all the good you do to the Daughters of Saint Anne, and for the kindness you showed me at once when I asked for the letter of recommendation.3

  4. May God therefore be thanked and blessed, who knows how to move the hearts of such worthy Pastors to give this most wretched servant of His proof that the Church appreciates our actions, though they are certainly not fit to correspond to what the good Jesus would require in His work through the most wretched of creatures. It is the least of all these who prostrates herself at the feet of Your Most Rev. Excellency and asks for your Pastoral blessing as she signs herself

Your Most Rev. Excellency's

Most devoted Servant Sr. Anna Rosa Gattorno

The Ladies of the «Pious Union» are complaining about the Sisters' management and accuse them of stinting the servant girls' food. Most Rev. Eminence,

  1. Where can I turn amid the tribulations in which I am immersed, if not to the feet of my Superior, where I have always found comfort and peace?

  2. I hear that the Ladies of the «Pious Union» are complaining about the conduct of the poor Daughters of Saint Anne.1

  3. It would take too long to say all there is to say about this. Most Rev. Eminence, I can only assure you that for two years we have served that «Pious Union» without the least pay or reward;2 the only reason that led us to such a sacrifice was so that the Marchioness Cavalletti would stay, as I am under so many obligations to that most worthy Marchioness; but hearing that she too is resigning, I have asked her to join my resignation to hers, as I so much want to be freed from it.3

  4. Oh my God!... Most Rev. Eminence, how can they make such an accusation, that we made the poor servant girls suffer in order to keep ourselves! Ah! it cannot be! One proof is that these poor girls write to me, and so do other people, saying they cannot bear to see the sisters suffer.

  5. Enough! All crosses are too dear to me, and I embrace this one too.

  6. The Marchioness had undertaken to inform Your Eminence and tell you everything,4 but I am not satisfied unless I

fulfil this duty myself, in my own hand,5 coming thereby to humble myself at your Feet and ask your Pastoral blessing, while deeply prostrate I remain Your Most Rev. Eminence's

Most humble Servant Sr. Anna Rosa Gattorno

She thanks him for the letter of recommendation and sends him the Rules.1

Most Rev. Excellency,

1. I thank you infinitely for the very beautiful letter you deigned to send me, in which you charitably praised those poor daughters of Saint Anne who have had the good fortune to be numbered in your flock, highlighting in your immense kindness what is to the credit of us poor creatures.2 Having nothing but prayer with which to repay such charity, the Daughters of Saint Anne will never fail to offer it, remembering Your Excellency as our distinguished Protector. I am sending you our Rules; read them at your leisure and don't trouble to return them; you can do so when an opportunity arises.

Prostrate at your Feet I ask your Pastoral Blessing, while with the greatest veneration I remain

Your humble and most devoted Servant Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

His letters are welcome. She has asked the Bishop of Imola for a letter of «recommendation» and is waiting for it; she has received others from Bishops. She invites him to Piacenza.1

Most worthy Count,

  1. Only today have I been able to read your letter, as I have been away from Piacenza. You tell me your letters will be a burden for me to read. Oh! my God! how can that be? So great a Protector of mine!2 Ah! no, they are too dear to me. Count, if my proposal were not too bold, I would ask you for one every day.

  2. I have written to the Bishop of Imola for the letter of recommendation;3 I hope that this charitable Pastor will grant my poor prayers and send me the letter I want.4 I have already received several, all very fine, beyond the merits of the Daughters of Saint Anne.

  3. I hear you are going to Bologna; may I hope that you will make a quick trip to Piacenza to visit this poor woman? What a lovely present that would be!!!

I dare not say more; I leave Saint Anne to plead for me. In haste, your

Humble Devoted Servant Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

4. P.S. Please give my respectful greetings to the C.ss your Mother and your sister.5

She will send the nursing sisters at once. She is to urge observance on them all. The President from Ovada will arrive with his housekeeper; she is to put them both up in the house and treat them with consideration.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I have received your letter and hear what you say about the nurses; I am sending them at once; you will receive them on Wednesday at 12, that is, the 13th of this month; go and fetch them at once, do you understand?1

  2. For the rest greet all the sisters for me and tell them to concentrate on being observant and to pray for the one who calls herself the least of them, this very poor Mother of yours.2 You, my daughter, take courage, and always keep your eyes fixed on the Rule so as to have it put fully into practice.3

Goodbye, your affect. M.R.

She forwards to him the «letters of recommendation» received from the Bishops, and will send the others when she has them.1

Most Rev. Eminence,

  1. Knowing how welcome to you is news of the Institute you protect with such kindness and charity, I hasten to send you the letters of Recommendation received from the Bishops where our houses are; they are only some of them;1 but I am asking for them, and as they are granted I shall send them to you, as is my duty.2

  2. Allow me to take this opportunity to thank you for all the alms and protection you give us poor daughters of Saint Anne; with ardent prayers we ask our August Saint to preserve you to us for many years, full of life and prosperity. Bless me together with the Institute, and kissing your ring with all devotion and respect, I remain Your Most Reverend Eminence's

Most humble Servant Sr. Anna Rosa Gattorno

She is sending her a sister cook. Various instructions. She has received the bolsters, thanks her and tells her not to send any more, as the Piacenza house is well supplied.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I hear you really need a cook; well, here she is; I hope she will do well, and send Sr. A. Emilia back to her former post;1 and as I wrote to you about Sr. A. Teresa, she does very well with the little boys, for teaching them their prayers and keeping them good has always been her daily bread; so she will be Sr. A. Innocenza's assistant.2 In this way this poor sister will be in a post where she will not have to go out; keep her cheerful, I would not want her to become downcast.

  2. For charity's sake, see whether the stockings have arrived, because there were 110 pairs;3 for charity's sake, I hope they have not gone astray.

  3. Today we received the basket; thank you for the chocolate; for charity's sake keep an eye on Sr. A. Apollonia, I commend her to you.4

  4. I hope providence will come to you; it will never fail if you are observant.

  5. I was displeased that you sent me the bolsters, when there are some here, and certainly more than in Genoa.5 Listen, when I said «I sleep well in it», I said it to thank you6 and to show you that I appreciated the bed you had prepared for me with such care, but certainly not because I lacked one here. Oh, daughter! You must not take my words so literally! So we understand each other for another time.

Goodbye. The Lord bless you and the whole Community. Goodbye, your affect. M.

She assigns two Sisters to her Community and advises her on the tasks they can do and how to deal with another Sister in the house. She urges observance and study of the Rules.1

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. Sr. A. Emilia will have come back to you from Genoa, and Sr. A. Teresa you will put in the school; she has poor eyesight but is a good sister who is always with the little boys and did well, because she teaches them very well to pray and to behave; so she can relieve Sr. A. Innocenza by looking after these boys;1 she cannot sew or knit, but she can also go out begging and help with the washing and certain heavy work; you will see she is good.2

  2. I hear what you tell me: send that sister to Genoa if need be, if you see that she will not submit. And the other one I gave you when I was in Genoa, whom I thought would be good for the school: if you see she is not doing well, tell her to be calm and get well, and then I shall try to place her elsewhere.3 Meanwhile look after her so that her ailments pass.

  3. For charity's sake, observance: Chapter every fortnight, the retreat, silence4 and the reading of the Rules, so that the Sisters learn them by heart and you may always be guided in every step and action by the holy words of our Rules. And I tell you that if you do this, Providence will never fail you.

  4. Pray well and fervently, always at the Community prayers, and at meditation too.5 I am glad to hear that the Priest is better; meanwhile you can go to confession to the Capuchins; do you understand? Goodbye, your

affect. M. R.

5. If you have any tomato preserve to spare,6 our cook Sr. A. Nazarena would need it, as she could not make any this year because all our tomatoes rotted; please. Goodbye.

She was only able to read his letter on returning home. She regrets not having been able to follow his advice, as the Marchioness Cavalletti had suggested that the Sisters withdraw from the work. She hopes to hand him the Bishops' letters of recommendation in person.

Most Rev. Eminence,

  1. On reaching Piacenza I found your esteemed letter, which comforted me amid so many tribulations;1 I am only sorry that I cannot carry out your suggestions, because the Marchioness Cavalletti had already advised the sisters to withdraw, finding it impossible to leave them there any longer, and she too asked to resign.2

  2. Most Rev. Eminence, how I suffered on hearing so many things said, none of them true; for what that house cost me is no small thing; enough, my God will see that everything comes to light and the disorders in that blessed Congregation are seen.3

  3. When I think that I was not in time to carry out your orders, I cannot help feeling the keenest regret; only a word from you could calm my sorrow.4

  4. Most Rev. Eminence, bless me, so that I may bear such severe tribulations and battles, and next January have the good fortune to come to your feet and hand you all the letters of Recommendation which the Bishops in whose dioceses we have houses deigned to send me, making the work of the Lord shine forth in them.5 With my head bowed to the ground I remain Your Most Rev. Eminence's

Most humble Servant Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

Thanks for his kindness to the Lugo Community, for which he asked and obtained a special blessing from the Holy Father Pius IX.1

Most Rev. Excellency,

  1. Allow me to address to Your Most Rev. Excellency two poorly written lines, because my illness does not allow me to write at length, and I wish to do so in my own hand. The reports2 I received from Lugo moved me deeply: Your Most Rev. Excellency so kindly went to visit those schools and brought them the Holy Father's blessing, not only by word of mouth but written in His Holiness's own hand. Oh! what a favour!

  2. The gratitude and thankfulness this unworthy servant of the Lord feels towards Your Most Rev. Excellency certainly cannot pass in silence, and I keenly desire to come soon to your feet so that I may thank Your Most Rev. Excellency for so signal a favour better in person than in writing. Meanwhile deign to grant me your Pastoral blessing, while prostrate with respect I remain, full of veneration, Your Most Rev. Excellency's

Humble and most devoted Servant Sr. Anna Rosa Gattorno

She approves what she says about the girls and urges her to arrange everything for the best and always in good harmony with the Superior.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I hear what you say about the school; as you suggest, do what is best regarding the girls, so that no difficulties arise.1 So try to arrange everything properly, in order and with precision, and always in agreement and good harmony with the Superior.2 I shall always approve whatever you do.

  2. Goodbye, yours in haste. I am so busy that I cannot find time to do and deal with the most urgent matters; your

affect. M. R. G.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I have received your little letter; your letters are always dear to me. I cannot understand how you can say I forget you; know that I write to no one as much as to Rome; I sent letters for everyone through Onorata;1 it is true that I did not send one for you in particular, but you must make allowances for someone with an immense amount of business who does not know which to deal with first.

  2. So, my daughter, how are you? For pity's sake take care of yourself; don't take so much quinine, because it does harm in the end;2 so take care of yourself.

  3. I hope we shall see each other soon, and then I shall tell you everything in person. Yes, my dearest daughter, I love you too much, and you must think of loving me as much as your

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I have just received your letter and hear what you say about the letters these good Parish Priests have written for you; well, meanwhile send me the ones you have, and send the others as they come.1

  2. I have received the certificate. Now it is up to you to see that the Rules are well observed, and so you will have Providence. Please watch over the sisters and listen carefully to the reports,2 and keep an eye on the one you know well is not very good.

Goodbye, the Lord bless you, and believe me ever your affect.

M. R.

Approval, encouragement and advice about the Community.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. All is well regarding the confessor; and as for the Sister, be a little patient and then we will send her to Ovada for a change of air: as soon as one who is there leaves, she will go. Tell her that meanwhile the air where she is is good, and that she should look after herself and do nothing.1

  1. You will have received a letter from Sr. A.   2. Meanwhile send me my accounts, so that I can have them paid and run up new ones afterwards.4 I await a letter from you saying: «the house is ready». I am in a hurry; your

[Most Rev. Chaplain,]

My daughter,

the very dear Signora Marianna.7 Listen, this Lady is used to being with the religious as if she were one of the household; treat her with familiarity. My daughter,

  1. Just a line to say that I want to know at once how Sr. A. Giulia feels and how long it is since she last had her periods.1 Write to me quite exactly.

your affect. M. R.

  2. Oh! blessed the soul who comes to be a delight to her God!2 A brief suffering for an eternity of joy.3 So, daughter, courage, and think of what you promised God in the persons of your Superiors.4

I cannot find words to tell you how sorry I was when it came to my mind that I should have sent Your Excellency as soon as possible1 the permissions granted by Rome for our Chapels, endorsed by our Curia of Piacenza, and that I had not done so. My daughter,

My daughter,

affect. M. R.

My daughter,

My daughter,

  1. This morning I received your letter with F. 35 inside, which you say is the money for the stockings.1 I hear with great pleasure that you always have sick people to nurse; God be blessed!

  2. I let you know that I hope to leave for Rome on the 15th of this month.2 If you need nurses you can tell me and I shall try to send you some.

Circular Letter

[My dearest daughters,]

  1. Behold, Sisters, the year now ended has been full of heavenly blessings for our poor Institute. The heavenly Father, who planted it in the garden of His Church, looks upon it with special favour. He has increased its houses and multiplied its members.

  2. Last year 5 new houses were opened2 and 46 sisters received the habit; and with the spread of the houses and the growth in sisters He has been pleased to strengthen it ever more in the spirit of its vocation.

  3. The Lord raised up our Institute to be the family of glorious Saint Anne, August Mother of Mary Immaculate, a family in which the great Saint would be honoured, loved and imitated.3 And on the whole the sisters answer to this purpose. They imitate the life their Holy Mother led on this earth for the good of her neighbour.

  4. The service they render the sick, both in hospitals and at home, is done with a spirit of faith and a love of sacrifice that clearly show they keep before their minds the divine words of Jesus Christ, who assures us that the care given to the sick for love of Him He counts as done to Himself.4

  1. No less watchful is the care of those employed in teaching to imitate the piety of our Holy Mother. They spend on it all the talent they have received from the Lord, so that their pupils may be good before God and before men; they bring them up dear to Jesus Christ and such as to be the comfort of their families.

  2. A sign of this spirit of their vocation that animates them is that, by God's goodness, they generally win the sympathy of the towns and villages where they work. Our Bishops have openly testified to this sympathy: in the Dioceses where we have houses they have issued the most cordial and expressive letters of recommendation, in which they speak highly of the sisters, of their zeal and of their wise and modest conduct, by which they edify their people.

  3. These letters of recommendation were to be presented to His Holiness, as indeed we have presented them.5

  4. Not only do the Bishops speak well of us, but we are also respected and honoured by the secular authorities; yet what crowns our joy is the love the Vicar of Jesus Christ bears our poor Institute.

  5. He shows this love by the frequent audiences he grants our sisters in Rome and the material aid he gives them;6 but we received a singular mark of affection on the 9th of this month, when we were at the audience.

  1. His Holiness welcomed us with singular signs of joy, received news of our Institute with particular interest, spoke encouraging words to us and showed us a token of familiar affection by giving us a fine basket of fruit. And finally, with all the fullness of his heart, he gave his fatherly Blessing to the whole Institute.

  2. Behold, sisters, how the loveliness of our Holy Mother, who drew them to herself, pours out upon us the affection of the heart of God, of the divine heart of Jesus and of Mary, and makes us objects of affection to heaven and to all the noblest creatures on earth.

  3. But the signs of affection of the Heavenly Father and of the Holy Mother would not have been complete had not tribulations been mingled with the consolations that accompanied our family in the year just ended; yes, the crosses that are the mark of God's chosen works were not lacking.

  4. Two in particular touched us deeply. These were the taking from us of the two sisters most zealous and hard-working in spreading the Institute and increasing its glory. You already understand me: we mourn the loss of Sister Anna Vincenza and Sister Anna Francesca;7 yes, we can bear witness that the love they had for increasing the splendour of their Holy Mother is what made them two victims and sacrificed them for the good of her family. But the Lord has willed it so; may His adorable will always be done.8

  1. Yet in so great a loss we have reason for comfort, namely that the example they have left us will spur us to imitate them and not be content until we can say: the love we had for our God, for the glory of the Holy Mother and for the spread of her Institute has taken our life.

  2. What gratitude does God ask of us for the favours with which He has filled us in the year now ended? He wants a deep sense of humility9 by which we confess that we have not deserved them. A humility that makes us offer Him all the praise the Institute receives from creatures, and confess before His Divine Majesty that we are His unprofitable servants and do not even manage to do what we are bound to do.

  3. The second thing He wants of us is that we be attentive to the observance of the Rules, and above all of the most important points; in particular I would mention punctuality in rising; on this observance depends the special blessing of the whole day. Samuel, because when called by the Lord early in the morning he answered the call promptly, saying, «Here I am, ready»! and rose at once, deserved to be chosen by the Lord as His Prophet; he deserved to be filled with His spirit and became a great saint.10 Rising is the first sacrifice He asks of us each day; if this sacrifice is made with the promptness He requires, it earns us a special grace to make our holy meditation well; and on a well-made meditation depends all our spiritual progress.

  4. To this end we urge the Superiors not to be quick to let sisters stay in bed in the morning for every trifling ailment, such as a little toothache, a slight headache, a mild rheumatism and similar discomforts. What harm those sisters do to their souls who, for such petty ailments, do not rise in the morning with the Community! My God! they deprive themselves of so many graces and lights that You give to those who make their meditation with the community at the appointed hour.

  5. Let the Superiors reflect that too much indulgence in letting a sister rest in the morning longer than the community is not true charity towards her, but should rather be called a cruelty11 towards her poor soul.

  1. Another very important thing for safeguarding virtue in the sisters is that the Superiors allow no one to answer the door except the sister given this office. It is likewise very important that the Superiors see to it that the sisters, when they go out, do not stop in the street and do not break the silence they must strictly keep.

  2. Let them also take great care that in the homes of the sick the sisters do not separate from one another except in cases of real necessity; and on returning home let them give an exact account.12

  3. If the Institute holds fast to these cardinal points of the rule, it will be a solid building that will not fear the assaults of its enemies, whether of the world or the demons of hell.13 It will be a joy to the Holy Mother, where she will be glorified, loved and imitated by her Daughters, and they will then merit at the end of their days the crown of glory the Lord has prepared for those who serve Him with a true heart.14

Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno15

  3. I trust that the Daughters of Saint Anne will do there too, as in all the other places2 where they are, all the good God grants them to do in fulfilling their duty, and that Your Most Ill. Excellency will be pleased to look after them,3 assuring you that the poor Daughters of Saint Anne will remember you in their prayers, imploring God's choicest blessings upon you; and the Institute will be most grateful for such protection, as will she who has the honour to remain

Your Most Ill. Excellency's

Most humble Servant Sr. Anna Rosa Gattorno

She sends her to stand in for the sick teacher and urges her to do everything well, as that school is closely watched.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I want you, on going to S. Martinello,1 to take courage and try to run the school well and confidently, and see that the M.sa2 is satisfied.

  2. So if the Inspector comes, tell him that the qualified Teacher cannot yet resume the school because she is under treatment (which is the plain truth). If he wants a doctor's certificate, we shall get him one.

  3. My daughter, I beg you: the good of the school and the honour of the Institute depend on you, as that school is closely watched.

  4. Goodbye; resting on your affection and good sense, I consider I have obtained everything for the good of our poor Institute.3

Goodbye; the Lord bless you, and ever your affect. M. R.
